claim: Large-conductance potassium (BK) channels have a large single-channel conductance of approximately 100–300 pS.
source: Large-conductance potassium (BK) channels are transmembrane (TM) proteins that can be synergistically and independently activated by membrane voltage and intracellular Ca2+. The only covalent connection between the cytosolic Ca2+ sensing domain and the TM pore and voltage sensing domains is a 15-residue 'C-linker'. To determine the linker's role in human BK activation, we designed a series of linker sequence scrambling mutants to suppress potential complex interplay of specific interactions with the rest of the protein. The results revealed a surprising sensitivity of BK activation to the linker sequence. Combining atomistic simulations and further mutagenesis experiments, we demonstrated that nonspecific interactions of the linker with membrane alone could directly modulate BK activation. The C-linker thus plays more direct roles in mediating allosteric coupling between BK domains than previously assumed. Our results suggest that covalent linkers could directly modulate TM protein function and should be considered an integral component of the sensing apparatus.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature (Knaus et al., 1996; Uebele et al., 2000; Salkoff et al., 2006; Lee and Cui, 2010; Yang et al., 2015) to support the conductance range.

claim: BK channels are activated by both intracellular Ca2+ and membrane voltage.
source: Large-conductance potassium (BK) channels are transmembrane (TM) proteins that can be synergistically and independently activated by membrane voltage and intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature (Shi and Cui, 2001; Horrigan and Aldrich, 2002; Gessner et al., 2012) to support dual activation mechanism.

claim: BK channels are involved in intracellular ion homeostasis and membrane excitation.
source: BK channels are involved in numerous vital physiological processes including intracellular ion homeostasis and membrane excitation, and are associated with pathogenesis of many diseases such as epilepsy, stroke, autism and hypertension (Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature (Zhou et al., 2017) to support the physiological roles.

claim: BK channels are associated with pathogenesis of epilepsy, stroke, autism and hypertension.
source: BK channels are involved in numerous vital physiological processes including intracellular ion homeostasis and membrane excitation, and are associated with pathogenesis of many diseases such as epilepsy, stroke, autism and hypertension (Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature (Zhou et al., 2017) to support disease associations.

claim: Functional BK channels are homo-tetramers.
source: Functional BK channels are homo-tetramers, each containing three distinct domains (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is established knowledge about BK channel structure.

claim: Each BK channel subunit contains three distinct domains: voltage sensor domain (VSD), pore-gate domain (PGD), and cytosolic tail domain (CTD).
source: Functional BK channels are homo-tetramers, each containing three distinct domains (Figure 1a). The voltage sensor domain (VSD) detects membrane potential, the pore-gate domain (PGD) controls the K+ selectivity and permeation, and the cytosolic tail domain (CTD) senses various intracellular ligands including Ca2+.
evidence: The manuscript describes the three domains and their functions, with reference to Figure 1a.

claim: The VSD and CTD form a Mg2+ binding site for Mg2+ dependent activation.
source: The VSD and the CTD also form a Mg2+ binding site for Mg2+ dependent activation (Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature (Yang et al., 2008) to support the Mg2+ binding site.

claim: The tetrameric assembly of CTD domains is referred to as the 'gating ring'.
source: The tetrameric assembly of CTD domains is also referred to as the 'gating ring'.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the manuscript.

claim: CTD of each BK subunit resides beneath the TMD of the neighboring subunit in a domain-swapped arrangement.
source: Previous studies on mouse BK channels (Yang et al., 2008) and recent atomistic structures of full-length Aplysia californica (aSlo1) and human BK channel (hSlo1) (Hite et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017; Tao and MacKinnon, 2019) reveal that CTD of each subunit reside beneath the TMD of the neighboring subunit in a surprising domain-swapped arrangement (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The manuscript cites published structures (Yang et al., 2008; Hite et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017; Tao and MacKinnon, 2019) and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The C-linker is a 15-residue peptide (R329 to K343 in human BK channel) that connects CTD and TMD.
source: The only covalent connection between CTD and TMD of BK channels is a 15-residue peptide referred to as the 'C-linker' (R329 to K343 in the human BK channel, hSlo1) (green in Figure 1a).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines the C-linker and its residue range.

claim: The C-linker directly connects the pore lining S6 helices in the PGD to the N-terminus of CTD (RCK1 N-lobe).
source: This linker directly connects the pore lining S6 helices in the PGD (yellow in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) to the N-terminus of CTD (known as RCK1 N-lobe; blue in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), and is believed to play an important role in mediating the gating ring-pore coupling (Gessner et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the structural connection with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and cites literature (Gessner et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2017).

claim: Lengthening the C-linker through inserting poly-AAG shifts voltage-dependent activation to more positive voltages (right shift in G-V curves).
source: For example, (Niu et al., 2004) observed that lengthening the C-linker through inserting poly-AAG (Supplementary file 1) was accompanied with right shifted voltage-dependent activation measured by conductance-voltage relations (G-V curves), while shortening the C-linker led to left-shifted G-V curves, clearly demonstrating the importance of C-linker in BK gating.
evidence: The manuscript cites published experimental results (Niu et al., 2004).

claim: Shortening the C-linker leads to left-shifted G-V curves.
source: For example, (Niu et al., 2004) observed that lengthening the C-linker through inserting poly-AAG (Supplementary file 1) was accompanied with right shifted voltage-dependent activation measured by conductance-voltage relations (G-V curves), while shortening the C-linker led to left-shifted G-V curves, clearly demonstrating the importance of C-linker in BK gating.
evidence: The manuscript cites published experimental results (Niu et al., 2004).

claim: V0.5 displayed a highly linear relationship with the number of residues inserted or deleted in the C-linker in the absence of Ca2+.
source: Intriguingly, the voltage required for half activation, V0.5, displayed a highly linear relationship with the number of residues inserted or deleted in the absence of Ca2+.
evidence: The manuscript describes a relationship observed in previous work (Niu et al., 2004).

claim: The linker-gating ring behaves as a 'passive spring' in activation of BK channels.
source: This led to the proposal that the linker-gating ring behaves as a 'passive spring' in activation of BK channels (Niu et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites a proposed model (Niu et al., 2004).

claim: Both Ca2+-free and bound Cryo-EM structures of full-length aSlo1 contain wide-open pores.
source: Both Ca2+-free and bound Cryo-EM structures of full-length aSlo1 (Hite et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017) were found to contain wide-open pores and thus did not provide clue to how the channel might be gated.
evidence: The manuscript cites published Cryo-EM structures (Hite et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017).

claim: The BK pore cavity becomes narrower, more elongated, and more hydrophobic in the metal-free state due to movement of pore-lining S6 helices.
source: Atomistic simulations later revealed that, due to the movement of pore-lining S6 helices (Figure 1b), the BK pore cavity become narrower, more elongated, and crucially, more hydrophobic in the metal-free state (i.e., without bound Ca2+ and Mg2+; presumably the closed state) (Jia et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published simulation results (Jia et al., 2018) and references Figure 1b.

claim: The BK pore can undergo hydrophobic dewetting transition to give rise to a vapor barrier that prevents ion permeation.
source: As such, the pore can readily undergo hydrophobic dewetting transition to give rise to a vapor barrier that prevents ion permeation (Jia et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published simulation results (Jia et al., 2018).

claim: Key movements of S6 helices involve bending at the glycine hinge (G310, G311) toward the membrane upon Ca2+ binding.
source: Specifically, key movements of S6 helices involve bending at the glycine hinge (G310, G311) toward the membrane upon Ca2+ binding (Figure 1b), leading to ~6 Å expansion of the pore entrance near I323.
evidence: The manuscript describes structural changes with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: S6 helix bending upon Ca2+ binding leads to approximately 6 Å expansion of the pore entrance near I323.
source: Specifically, key movements of S6 helices involve bending at the glycine hinge (G310, G311) toward the membrane upon Ca2+ binding (Figure 1b), leading to ~6 Å expansion of the pore entrance near I323.
evidence: The manuscript describes structural changes with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: BK channels may be gated at the selectivity filter.
source: It has also been proposed that BK channels may be gated at the selectivity filter (Wilkens and Aldrich, 2006; Kopec et al., 2019; Schewe et al., 2019), the conformation of which could be modulated by the S6 helix orientation.
evidence: The manuscript cites published proposals (Wilkens and Aldrich, 2006; Kopec et al., 2019; Schewe et al., 2019).

claim: The R329KK331 residues in the C-linker form alternating interactions with E321 and E224 from neighboring chains and membrane lipids during each gating cycle.
source: The notion that interactions of C-linkers can modulate BK activation has actually been demonstrated in a recent study, where the R329KK331 residues in the C-linker was proposed to form alternating interactions with E321 and E224 from the neighboring chains and membrane lipids during each gating cycle (Tian et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Tian et al., 2019).

claim: C-linker sequence scrambling dramatically modulates BK voltage activation.
source: Importantly, as shown in Figure 1d and Table 1, V0.5 depends very sensitively on the C-linker sequence, which is in line with previous observations (Soom et al., 2008). All five mutants that lead to functional channels, K0, K1, K2, K4 and K7, have significantly altered activation voltage, with V0.5 changes as large as ~135 mV.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 1d and Table 1.

claim: K0, K1, K2, K4 and K7 C-linker scrambling mutants have significantly altered activation voltage, with V0.5 changes as large as approximately 135 mV.
source: All five mutants that lead to functional channels, K0, K1, K2, K4 and K7, have significantly altered activation voltage, with V0.5 changes as large as ~135 mV.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data.

claim: K3, K5 and K6 C-linker scrambling mutants did not show functional expression.
source: Among these mutants K3, K5 and K6 did not show functional expression, while other mutant channels showed robust currents (Figure 1c).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 1c and Table 1.

claim: The K0 mutation does not affect voltage sensor movements during voltage-dependent activation.
source: The results show that the K0 mutation gives rises to Q-V curves similar to that of the WT channels. This is in contrast to the G-V relation of the K0 mutation, which is shifted to more negative voltages by about −95 mV (Table 1). These results show that the K0 mutation does not affect voltage sensor movements, but may alter pore opening to modify BK channel activation.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental gating current data comparing K0 and WT.

claim: The K0 mutation may alter pore opening to modify BK channel activation.
source: These results show that the K0 mutation does not affect voltage sensor movements, but may alter pore opening to modify BK channel activation.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the gating current and G-V data.

claim: The C-linker is a structured loop with essentially identical conformations in both metal-free (closed) and metal-bound (open) states.
source: These structures reveal that the C-linker is a structured loop with essentially identical conformations in both metal-free (closed) and metal-bound (open) states (Figure 1b).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural analysis with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: The Cα root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of C-linker conformations between metal-free and metal-bound states is only approximately 0.8 Å.
source: The Cα root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of C-linker conformations between the two states is only ~0.8 Å.
evidence: The manuscript presents structural analysis data.

claim: The C-linker forms extensive contacts with the RCK1 N-lobe (H344 to N427) of the gating ring, mainly mediated by the Y332GGSYSA338 segment.
source: The linker forms extensive contacts with the RCK1 N-lobe (H344 to N427) of the gating ring, mainly mediated by the Y332GGSYSA338 segment in the C-linker, and S0' of VSD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural analysis with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The two conserved tyrosine residues (Y332 and Y336) are fully embedded in a hydrophobic RCK1 N-lobe pocket.
source: In particular, the two conserved tyrosine residues (Y332 and Y336) are fully embedded in a hydrophobic RCK1 N-lobe pocket, apparently maintaining a tight packing between the C-linker and RCK1 N-lobe (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural analysis with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Several positively charged residues (R329, K330, K331, R342 and K343) flank the Y332GGSYSA338 segment and are exposed to solvent.
source: Several positively charged residues (R329, K330, K331, R342 and K343) flank the above segment and are exposed to solvent, likely mediating the solvation of the C-linker.
evidence: The manuscript describes structural analysis.

claim: The C-linker maintained stable conformations and contacts with VSD and RCK1 N-lobe throughout 800 ns simulation time.
source: The stability of the C-linker conformation as a structured loop is further confirmed by atomistic molecular dynamic (MD) simulations, which showed that the C-linker maintained stable conformations and contacts with VSD and RCK1 N-lobe throughout the 800 ns simulation time (Figure 2a–b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4, WT).
evidence: The manuscript presents simulation data with references to multiple figures.

claim: The root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) of the C-linker region is approximately 1–2 Å.
source: The root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) of the C-linker region is ~1–2 Å, which is only slightly elevated compared to regions with helical or sheet secondary structures (Figure 2b).
evidence: The manuscript presents simulation data in Figure 2b.

claim: The end-to-end distance of the C-linker fluctuated stably around 30 Å in both metal-bound and free state simulations.
source: The end-to-end distance of the C-linker fluctuated stably ~30 Å in both metal-bound and free state simulations (Figure 2a), even as the pore underwent dewetting transitions in the metal-free state (Figure 2—figure supplement 4c).
evidence: The manuscript presents simulation data in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 4c.

claim: C-linker is the key pathway of dynamic coupling between the gating ring and PGD.
source: Dynamic network analysis further reveals that the C-linker is a key pathway of dynamic coupling between the gating ring and PGD.
evidence: The manuscript presents dynamic network analysis results.

claim: The main pathways of communication from Ca2+ and Mg2+ binding sites to the PGD go through the C-linker for all four chains.
source: The results reveal that the main pathways of communication from Ca2+ and Mg2+ binding sites to the PGD, go through the C-linker for all four chains (Figure 2c–d and Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript presents dynamic network analysis results with references to figures.

claim: In the metal-free state, the main path from the RCK2 Ca2+ binding site to PGD goes from the neighboring monomer in every other chain.
source: Interestingly though, in the metal-free state the main path from the RCK2 Ca2+ binding site to PGD goes from the neighboring monomer in every other chain (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: The manuscript presents dynamic network analysis results with references to Figure 2c–d.

claim: The changes in voltage dependent gating upon permutating linkers are unlikely to derive from a change in the overall structural features and dynamical properties of BK channel.
source: Atomistic simulations suggest that the changes in voltage dependent gating upon permutating linkers are unlikely to derive from a change in the overall structural features and dynamical properties of BK channel.
evidence: The manuscript presents simulation analysis.

claim: The overall RMSD of mutant channels is below approximately 5 Å and the TM domain (core) RMSD is around 2–3 Å from the initial cryo-EM-derived structures.
source: The structure of the channel appears minimally perturbed by the mutated linkers, with the overall RMSD below ~5 Å and the TM domain (core) RMSD around 2–3 Å from the initial cryo-EM-derived structures for both WT and mutant channels (Figure 2—figure supplement 4a–b).
evidence: The manuscript presents simulation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4a–b.

claim: All mutant channels can readily undergo hydrophobic dewetting transitions as observed for the WT channel.
source: All mutant channels can readily undergo hydrophobic dewetting transitions as observed for the WT channel (Figure 2—figure supplement 4c).
evidence: The manuscript presents simulation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4c.

claim: The linker region maintains similar backbone conformations in WT and all mutants.
source: The linker region also maintains similar backbone conformations in WT and all mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), even though it becomes slightly more dynamic in the K7 mutant as reflected in the RMSF profile (Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: The manuscript presents simulation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Scrambling mutations do not appear to perturb long-range coupling properties; the C-linker remains to provide the key pathway of dynamic coupling between CTD and PGD.
source: Furthermore, scrambling mutations do not appear to perturb long-range coupling properties either; the C-linker remains to provide the key pathway of dynamic coupling between CTD and PGD.
evidence: The manuscript presents simulation analysis.

claim: V0.5 of linker scrambling mutants is not correlated with the inherent linker extension.
source: The results suggest that V0.5 of linker scrambling mutants is not correlated with the inherent linker extension (Figure 2—figure supplement 6) and is inconsistent with the prediction based on the previous linker-gating ring passive spring model (Niu et al., 2004) (dashed line in Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The manuscript presents simulation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The C-linker does not have any contact with the putative gating charges of BK VSD (R207, R210 and R213).
source: Contact analysis show that the C-linker does not have any contact with the putative gating charges of BK VSD (R207, R210 and R213) and thus unlikely interfere with potential lipid-VSD interactions.
evidence: The manuscript presents contact analysis from simulations.

claim: The measured V0.5 shows a strong correlation with the sequence separation between E324 and the nearest C-linker Tyr residue in both 0 [Ca2+]i and 100 µM [Ca2+]i.
source: Indeed, the measured V0.5 shows a strong correlation with the sequence separation between E324 (the approximate location of membrane interface) and the nearest C-linker Tyr residue (Figure 3b) in both 0 [Ca2+]I and 100 µM [Ca2+]i.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 3b.

claim: Positioning Tyr residue closer to the membrane interface could allow stronger membrane anchoring, preferentially stabilizing the bent conformation of S6 in the open state.
source: Positioning this Tyr residue closer to the membrane interface could allow stronger membrane anchoring, preferentially stabilizing the bent conformation of S6 in the open state and shifting the equilibrium toward the active state of the channel as observed.
evidence: The manuscript infers this mechanism from the correlation between Tyr position and V0.5.

claim: The interaction between the Tyr residue and the membrane does not alter Ca2+ dependent activation.
source: This effect is not affected by the change of [Ca2+]i, suggesting that the interaction between the Tyr residue and the membrane does not alter Ca2+ dependent activation.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation that the correlation holds at both 0 and 100 µM Ca2+.

claim: Positioning of the C-linker in the metal-bound state allows more extensive interactions between Tyr sidechains and the membrane interface.
source: Importantly, results from simulation analysis confirm that positioning of the C-linker in the metal-bound state allows more extensive interactions between Try sidechains and the membrane interface (e.g., compare Figure 4a vs b and c vs d), which would stabilize the open state and thus lower the voltage required for activation.
evidence: The manuscript presents simulation data in Figure 4.

claim: Placing Tyr closer to the end of the S6 helix allows more extensive Tyr/membrane interface interactions, forming larger numbers of polar and nonpolar interactions on average.
source: Consistent with our experimental data, placing Tyr closer to the end of the S6 helix shifts V0.5 (Figure 1c–d and Figure 3) indeed allows more extensive Tyr/membrane interface interactions, forming larger numbers of polar and nonpolar interactions on average (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript presents simulation data in Figure 5.

claim: Y329 of K7 appears to be dominated by extensive π-cation interactions in the metal-bound state.
source: Note that Y329 of K7 appears to be dominated by extensive π-cation interactions in the metal-bound state (Figure 5d, comparing empty and filled bars) and as a consequence forms slightly fewer hydrogen bonding interactions on average (Figure 5b).
evidence: The manuscript presents simulation data in Figure 5.

claim: The effects of C-linker sequence scrambling on voltage gating persist in Core-MT constructs where the gating ring is completely removed.
source: If the observed effects on the voltage gating of full-length BK channels are indeed mainly due to the nonspecific interactions between the C-linker and membrane interface, they should persist in the Core-MT truncated channel (Budelli et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2017), in which the whole gating-ring is removed and there is no CTD coupling with either VSD or PGD via the C-linker (Budelli et al., 2013; Figure 6a). To test this prediction, Core-MT channels with three C-linker scrambling mutations, K0, K2 and K7, were expressed (Figure 6b) and their voltage-dependent activation measured. Mutations of the C-linker shifted the G-V relation of the Core-MT constructs in the same directions as observed for the full-length channels (Table 1), with K0 and K7 stabilizing channel activation (Figure 6c,e) while K2 making activation at higher voltages (Figure 6d).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 6 and Table 1.

claim: The reduction in the activation voltage by K0 mutation is only approximately 42 mV in Core-MT, compared to approximately 94 mV in the full-length channel.
source: However, the reduction in the activation voltage by K0 mutation is only ~42 mV in Core-MT, compared to ~94 mV in the full-length channel (Figure 6c), and for K7 mutation is ~67 mV in Core-MT, compared to ~135 mV in the full-length channel (Figure 6e).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 6c and 6e.

claim: The reduction in the activation voltage by K7 mutation is approximately 67 mV in Core-MT, compared to approximately 135 mV in the full-length channel.
source: However, the reduction in the activation voltage by K0 mutation is only ~42 mV in Core-MT, compared to ~94 mV in the full-length channel (Figure 6c), and for K7 mutation is ~67 mV in Core-MT, compared to ~135 mV in the full-length channel (Figure 6e).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 6e.

claim: The C-linker is more flexible in the absence of the gating ring, thus weakening the effects of membrane anchoring.
source: This is not considered surprising as the C-linker is more flexible in the absence of the gating ring, thus weakening the effects of membrane anchoring.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the reduced magnitude of V0.5 shifts in Core-MT constructs.

claim: The K0 mutation in Core-MT does not affect voltage sensor movements.
source: We measured the gating currents of the Core-MT and the K0 mutant in Core-MT (Figure 6f). The Q-V curves for these two channels are similar (Figure 6g) supporting that the K0 mutation does not affect voltage sensor movements, but may alter pore opening to modify BK channel activation.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental gating current data in Figure 6f and 6g.

claim: K0 Y330G mutation abolished the effects of K0 on G-V relation and largely shifted the G-V back to that of the WT.
source: Strikingly, K0 Y330G mutation abolished the effects of K0 on G-V relation and largely shifted the G-V back to that of the WT, with a V0.5 of 169.8 ± 5.0 mV as compared to 183.4 ± 3.2 mV for the WT (Figure 7b).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 7b.

claim: Membrane anchoring effects of Tyr are mainly responsible for modulating the activation voltage in the C-linker sequence scrambling mutants.
source: This, together with the correlation shown in Figure 3, provides a direct support that membrane anchoring effects of Tyr are mainly responsible for modulating the activation voltage in the C-linker sequence scrambling mutants.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the Y330G rescue experiment and the correlation data.

claim: Nonspecific interactions of the C-linker with membrane alone could directly modulate BK activation.
source: Combining atomistic simulations and further mutagenesis experiments, we demonstrated that nonspecific interactions of the linker with membrane alone could directly modulate BK activation.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The C-linker plays more direct roles in mediating allosteric coupling between BK domains than previously assumed.
source: The C-linker thus plays more direct roles in mediating allosteric coupling between BK domains than previously assumed.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Covalent linkers could directly modulate TM protein function and should be considered an integral component of the sensing apparatus.
source: Our results suggest that covalent linkers could directly modulate TM protein function and should be considered an integral component of the sensing apparatus.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The V0.5 of WT Core-MT is only approximately 52 mV larger than the full-length BK channel.
source: Since the whole gating ring is removed, the Core-MT construct should correspond to a state where the passive spring is fully relaxed and thus V0.5 maximizes. Yet, the V0.5 of WT Core-MT is only ~52 mV larger than the full-length BK channel (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Table 1.

claim: The poly-AAG insertion site locates in a short loop following the C-linker segment -Y332GGSY336- that forms stable contacts with RCK1 N-lobe.
source: For example, the Cryo-EM structures of BK channels (Hite et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017) reveal that the previously published poly-AAG insertion site (Niu et al., 2004), right after residue S337 (Supplementary file 1), actually locates in a short loop following the C-linker segment -Y332GGSY336- that forms stable contacts with RCK1 N-lobe (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural analysis with references to published structures (Hite et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017; Niu et al., 2004) and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The inserted residues in poly-AAG insertion mutants would project away from the channel and are very unlikely to affect the effective C-linker length.
source: The inserted residues would project away from the channel (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), and are very unlikely to affect the effective C-linker length (or the gating ring-pore distance) as originally designed.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from structural analysis with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: β subunits make extensive contacts with the C-linker for influencing the channel gating and manipulating the channel function.
source: Interestingly, the recently published Cryo-EM structures confirms that β subunits make extensive contacts with the C-linker for influencing the channel gating and manipulating the channel function (Tao and MacKinnon, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites published Cryo-EM structures (Tao and MacKinnon, 2019).

claim: Homology models of WT hSlo1 based on aSlo1 Cryo-EM structures are essentially identical to the actual hSlo1 structures, with the central PGD structures differing by only 0.87 Å.
source: The homology models have been cross validated using Cryo-EM structures of hSlo1 that became available after the completion of this work (Tao and MacKinnon, 2019). The results show that aS1o1-derived models are essentially identical to the actual hSlo1 structures, with the central PGD structures differ by only 0.87 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents structural comparison data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

source: The backbone RMSD between the model and new structure is only 2.18 Å at the whole channel level and as low as 0.87 Å in the PGD.
evidence: The manuscript presents structural comparison data.

claim: Aromatic amino acids such as Tyr and Trp are 'membrane anchoring', with a strong preference toward localizing at the membrane-water interface.
source: Among various amino acids, aromatic ones such as Tyr and Trp are known to be 'membrane anchoring', with a strong preference toward localizing at the membrane-water interface (Johansson and Lindahl, 2006; Monticelli et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature (Johansson and Lindahl, 2006; Monticelli et al., 2008).

claim: Tyr sidechains can embed their aromatic rings in the lipid tail region and direct the polar -OH groups toward the lipid headgroup region to form hydrogen bonding interactions with water and lipid headgroups.
source: As illustrated in Figure 4, Tyr sidechains contain both aromatic rings and polar groups that allow them to embed their aromatic rings in the lipid tail region and at the same time direct the polar -OH groups toward the lipid headgroup region to form hydrogen bonding interactions with water and lipid headgroups (Johansson and Lindahl, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript describes Tyr-membrane interactions with reference to Figure 4 and cites literature (Johansson and Lindahl, 2006).

claim: The aromatic ring of Tyr could form π-cation interactions with positively charged cholines in lipid headgroups.
source: In addition, the aromatic ring could also form π-cation interactions with positively charged cholines in lipid headgroups (Roberts et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature (Roberts et al., 2018).

claim: The Tyr-membrane interactions primarily promote gate opening rather than affecting coupling between sensors and pore.
source: However, since the C-linker is important for the coupling of the pore with both Ca2+ and voltage sensors, we expect that the C-linker scrambling mutations would have altered both Ca2+ and voltage-dependent activation if they were to primarily affect coupling. Since these mutations have little effect on Ca2+ dependent activation (Figure 3), it seems that the Tyr-membrane interactions primarily promote gate opening.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation that mutations affect voltage but not Ca2+ dependent activation.

claim: The gating ring has some influence on the functional effects of the C-linker mutations.
source: We notice that the gating ring has some influence on the functional effects of the mutations (Figures 1 and 6, Table 1), these effects may be due to the conformational restraints imposed by the gating ring on the C-linker, but such restraints may not be sensitive to conformational changes caused by Ca2+ binding.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from comparing full-length and Core-MT data.

claim: The C-linker is unlikely an inert component of the linker-gating ring 'passive spring'.
source: Our conclusion that the C-linker is unlikely an inert component of the linker-gating ring 'passive spring' is also consistent with other structural and functional studies of BK channels.
